# 1 Clement — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Clement of Rome (traditional); anonymous letter of the Roman church |
| **Date** | c. 96–98 CE |
| **Audience** | The church at Corinth, experiencing a leadership revolt |
| **Genre** | Pastoral letter / early homily |
| **Timeline** | Written under Domitian or just after; contemporary with Revelation |
| **In One Sentence** | A long, authoritative letter from Rome to Corinth demanding the reinstatement of deposed elders — and in doing so, laying the first foundations of Roman ecclesial primacy and apostolic succession. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

The year is approximately 96 CE. The Roman emperor Domitian has just died, ending a reign that many Christians experienced as persecution. The church at Corinth — Paul's most turbulent community, if his letters are any guide — is in crisis again. A group of younger members has ousted the established elders, apparently for reasons that are not entirely clear. Word has reached Rome, and Rome is not pleased.

What is remarkable is not just that Rome responds, but how Rome responds: with a letter of extraordinary length (it is longer than many books of the New Testament), packed with Old Testament citation, philosophical argument, illustrations from nature and military discipline, and a tone of serene, immovable authority. The letter never identifies its author. It speaks throughout as the voice of the Roman church itself: "The church of God which sojourns at Rome to the church of God which sojourns at Corinth." This corporate authorial voice is itself a theological statement: the Roman community is not lecturing as one individual to another, but as a sister church exercising a kind of pastoral oversight.

The letter was written in Greek — the lingua franca of Mediterranean Christianity — and reveals an author or authors of considerable education: familiar with Stoic philosophy, with the rhetoric of the Hellenistic letter tradition, with the Septuagint in depth, and with the Pauline letters. The world behind the text is one where Christians are navigating between Jewish scripture, Greek philosophical categories, Roman administrative structures, and the memory of the apostolic generation that is just passing from living memory.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The immediate occasion is the Corinthian schism. A faction has removed the duly appointed elders (presbyteroi/episkopoi — the letter uses both terms) from their offices, apparently without the elders having done anything to merit removal. The Roman church regards this as an intolerable breach of order (Greek: taxis), and the letter is a sustained argument for why God's world runs on properly established order, why that order in the church traces back through the apostles to Christ and through Christ to God, and why the Corinthians must restore the deposed men immediately.

But the letter has a second, more historically momentous purpose that is woven through it rather than stated directly: it is the first known exercise of Roman oversight over another church. Rome is not merely offering advice. The letter assumes that its judgment should be heeded, that Corinth has some kind of accountability to Rome, and that failure to comply will be morally serious. Chapter 59 opens the Great Prayer — a magnificent liturgical composition — and chapter 63 concludes the body of the letter with the words: "You will give us joy and gladness if you are obedient to the things we have written through the Holy Spirit." The claim is breathtaking in its confidence.

A third purpose is memorial. Chapters 5–6 contain the earliest surviving account of the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul, and the statement that these deaths happened "among us" (i.e., in Rome) is the oldest evidence we have that both apostles died in Rome. The letter was written when people who remembered Peter and Paul were still alive, or had just died. The memory is fresh, and the author invokes it with genuine grief: they "contended unto death" and are the "greatest and most righteous pillars" of the church.

---

## How to Read This Book

First Clement is long — 65 chapters — and rewards reading in sections rather than all at once. Think of it in five movements.

Chapters 1–3 are the occasion: an account of Corinth's former virtues, followed by the painful report of their present "abominable and unholy sedition." The contrast is sharp and deliberate.

Chapters 4–39 are the great argument from example. The author piles up illustrations of humility, obedience, and the dangers of envy and strife — drawing from Cain and Abel, Jacob and Esau, the wilderness generation, David, Elijah, Job, and then the apostles and martyrs. Chapter 25 contains the famous Phoenix passage, where the author treats the legend of the phoenix (the bird that rises from its own ashes every 500 years in Arabia) as a genuine natural fact that proves the resurrection. This is not allegory for him — he believes the phoenix is real. It is a charming window into ancient science.

Chapters 40–44 are the heart of the letter's ecclesiology: the argument for apostolic succession. "The apostles received the gospel for us from the Lord Jesus Christ; Jesus Christ was sent from God. Christ therefore is from God, and the apostles are from Christ ... the apostles knew through our Lord Jesus Christ that there would be strife over the name of bishop. For this reason, therefore, having received complete foreknowledge, they appointed the above-mentioned, and afterwards gave them a permanent character, so that if these should fall asleep, other approved men should succeed to their ministry." This is the founding document of the apostolic succession doctrine.

Chapters 59–61 contain the Great Prayer — one of the most magnificent pieces of early Christian liturgical prose. Modeled on Jewish synagogue prayer, it intercedes for rulers, the sick, the hungry, and the whole cosmos. Read it slowly. It is more beautiful than most of what the New Testament contains liturgically.

Chapter 65 is a brief, urgent closing: restore the men, send back our messengers with good news, and do it quickly.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

First Clement is in direct conversation with Paul's two letters to the Corinthians. The author knows 1 Corinthians well — he quotes it explicitly — and his letter is in some ways a third intervention in the same intractable community that Paul had wrestled with forty years earlier. The recurrence of division at Corinth is striking: Paul diagnosed it as a problem of loyalty to competing teachers (1 Cor 1:12); 1 Clement diagnoses it as a problem of disordered ambition displacing legitimate authority. Same city, same structural problem, different analysis.

The letter's doctrine of apostolic succession (chapters 42–44) becomes the backbone of Ignatius of Antioch's letters (written perhaps 15 years later), which push the monarchical episcopate even further. The trajectory from 1 Clement to Ignatius to Irenaeus of Lyon is the direct line of development of Catholic ecclesiology.

The Great Prayer (chapters 59–61) is the strongest surviving evidence that early Christian prayer was deeply indebted to Jewish synagogue liturgy (specifically the Amidah/Shemoneh Esreh). It connects to the Didache's Eucharistic prayers and to the later developed liturgies of East and West.

The letter's interest in "order" (taxis) reflects Stoic philosophical categories — the cosmos as a perfectly ordered system — and connects 1 Clement to the broader project of early Christian intellectual engagement with Hellenistic philosophy, a conversation that reaches its fullest expression in Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The letter's argument is built almost entirely from the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament). Modern readers who don't know the LXX well will miss how saturated the argument is: the author is not merely citing proof-texts but inhabiting a world in which Isaiah, Psalms, Job, and the Pentateuch are the primary vocabulary for understanding the present crisis. The Corinthian schism is read through the lens of Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16), of Saul's envy of David, of Cain's murder of Abel. The typological method is pervasive and needs to be recognized.

The Phoenix passage (chapter 25) will strike modern readers as embarrassing, but it reveals something important: the author's epistemology makes no sharp distinction between natural philosophy and theological argument. If the Phoenix is a documented fact of natural history (which Greek writers like Herodotus and Pliny accepted), then it is legitimate evidence for the resurrection. This is not naive — it is a coherent ancient methodology in which the whole natural world is a book of theological truths.

The letter's address to the Corinthians never claims legal authority over them. The authority it claims is harder to name: it is the authority of seniority, of apostolic connection, of corporate wisdom, and of the Holy Spirit speaking through the Roman church. Modern readers in Protestant traditions may be startled by how early and how confidently Roman ecclesiastical authority is asserted — and by how far the letter stops short of the language that would later develop into papal supremacy.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

First Clement was almost canonical — and in some communities it may have functioned as such. It was included in the fifth-century Codex Alexandrinus (one of the four great uncial New Testament manuscripts), appended after Revelation. It appears in the canon lists of some early Eastern churches. Eusebius (c. 313 CE) considered it genuinely apostolic and "acknowledged."

What excluded it was not doubt about its content but doubt about its apostolic authorship. The letter does not claim to be written by Clement — it does not name its author at all. The attribution to Clement of Rome (traditionally the third or fourth bishop of Rome after Peter) comes from Dionysius of Corinth writing around 170 CE. By the time canonical decisions were being firmly made (late fourth century), the pseudonymity problem — combined with the existence of a much larger corpus of firmly canonical texts — made inclusion unnecessary even for those who revered the letter.

The Eastern Orthodox Church treats 1 Clement as a highly significant patristic text. The Roman Catholic Church has always honored it as an early expression of Roman primacy, though it is not scripture. Protestant churches from the Reformation onward have used it extensively in debates about polity, succession, and ecclesiology — both sides of the episcopal/presbyterian debate claim it.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| c. 64–68 CE | Deaths of Peter and Paul in Rome (referenced in ch. 5–6) |
| c. 68–96 CE | Growing Roman church; Domitian's reign and possible persecution |
| c. 96–98 CE | 1 Clement written in response to Corinthian schism |
| c. 110–117 CE | Ignatius of Antioch's letters build on 1 Clement's ecclesiology |
| c. 170 CE | Dionysius of Corinth first names Clement as author |
| c. 313 CE | Eusebius lists 1 Clement as "acknowledged" and genuine |
| c. 367 CE | Athanasius excludes it from his NT canon list |
| c. 400 CE | Included in Codex Alexandrinus after Revelation |
| c. 1628 CE | Codex Alexandrinus brought to England; 1 Clement rediscovered by West |
| 1875 CE | Complete Greek text discovered and published by Bryennios |

---
